passage:
Swati's eyes did not leave the screen, even when Papa held out her shoes. The school van would be at the gate soon.
"Two more songs, then the cartoon goes off," said Yogesh, crouching beside her. "After that, we race to the door. Who is faster in socks?"
The last song ended and Yogesh pressed the button. Swati's lip shook. "No! I want the rest!" She gripped the remote.
He kept his voice soft. "I know it's hard to stop. It will be here this evening. Come, let's hop like frogs to the door."
She sniffled, hopped once, and looked back at the dark screen.

qa.q: What did Yogesh suggest doing after the cartoon went off?
qa.a: He suggested a race to the door, then hopping like frogs to the door.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when the last song ended?
qa.a: She was upset and felt as if she was losing something she loved: her lip shook and she gripped the remote.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's approach work at least partly?
qa.a: He gave a warning, kept a clear limit, and offered a fun next thing, so she had something to move towards. 🙂

qa.q: How does Yogesh seem to see Swati's tears?
qa.a: He treats them as real difficulty stopping, not naughtiness, since he speaks softly and says it is hard.

grounding: A child cannot stop watching cartoons and is upset when it ends; the parent sets clear time, gives a warning and offers a fun next thing.

passage: In their Stockholm flat, Wei sat nose to the screen, watching the rabbit cartoon. Oskar, his dad, knelt beside him. "Two more minutes, then off. After that, we build the pillow fort." Wei didn't even blink. When the timer beeped and Oskar switched it off, Wei wailed. "Nooo! It wasn't finished!" He flung himself onto the rug as if something had been stolen. Oskar sat down. "It's hard to stop. The rabbit will be there tomorrow." He grabbed two cushions. "Fort's waiting." Wei peeked. Then he crawled over and pushed a cushion into the wall.

qa.q: What did Oskar promise after the cartoon?
qa.a: He promised they would build the pillow fort.

qa.q: Why did Wei wail when the screen went off?
qa.a: He felt upset and robbed, as if switching off meant losing something, because the cartoon held him so tightly.

qa.q: What did Oskar do that helps with switching off?
qa.a: He gave a clear two-minute warning, stayed calm, and offered a fun next thing, the pillow fort.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel when Wei crawls over to build?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved that the warning and the fort worked without a battle.

grounding: A young boy is upset when his cartoon ends, and his father gives a warning, a clear limit and a fun next thing.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was glued to the cartoon on her mother's phone. When the nurse called another name, Neelam said, "Pooja, one more song, then phone off. Then we play I-spy." Pooja nodded without looking up. The song ended. Neelam took the phone. Pooja's face crumpled and she kicked the chair. "Give it! I want it!" Neelam kept her voice soft. "It's hard to stop. I spy with my little eye... something red." Pooja sniffed. She looked around. "The fire extinguisher?" "Yes!" Pooja wiped her nose. "My turn."

qa.q: What was the first thing Neelam spied?
qa.a: Something red, which Pooja guessed was the fire extinguisher.

qa.q: How was Pooja feeling when she kicked the chair?
qa.a: She felt upset and angry, as if losing the cartoon meant losing something she loved.

qa.q: Which parts of Neelam's approach helped Pooja switch off?
qa.a: She gave a clear warning, stayed calm and soft, and moved straight to a fun next thing, I-spy.

qa.q: What would change if Neelam gave the phone back when Pooja kicked?
qa.a: Pooja would learn that getting upset brings the screen back, making every switch-off harder.

grounding: A young girl struggles to stop watching cartoons in a waiting room, and her mother gives a warning, holds the limit and offers a game.
